title: UNFCCC, Kyoto and the Paris Agreement

cards.h: Treaty facts are Prelims and Mains staples
cards.b:
UPSC asks for the year, the principle and the difference between Kyoto and Paris. Mains asks if the system is fair and working.

Master the timeline and the three principles: CBDR-RC, precaution, sustainable development.

Adopted at the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and in force from 21 March 1994. Nearly all countries (about 198 parties) have joined. It states the goal of stabilising greenhouse gases at a safe level. The COP is its supreme body and meets yearly.

Annex I lists developed countries and economies in transition. Annex II lists rich countries that must give finance and technology. Others are non-Annex I, including India and China.

Adopted in 1997, in force 2005. Only Annex I countries had legally binding targets: about 5 percent below 1990 levels in the first period (2008–12). The Doha Amendment (2012) set a second period for 2013–20.

Flexible tools: emissions trading, Joint Implementation and the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM). The US never ratified; Canada withdrew in 2011. Kyoto covered a shrinking share of global emissions.

• Bali Action Plan (2007).
  • Copenhagen (2009): the $100 billion a year pledge and the 2 °C goal, but not binding.
  • Cancun (2010): Green Climate Fund created.
  • Durban (2011): talks for a new universal deal.
  • Lima (2014): intended nationally determined contributions (INDCs).

Adopted on 12 December 2015 at COP21 and in force on 4 November 2016. It is universal and legally binding on process, not on targets.

Goal: keep warming well below 2 °C, pursue 1.5 °C, reach peak and then balance of sources and sinks in the second half of the century, and align finance. Each country sets its own Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and renews it every five years with a ratchet (no backsliding).

• Article 6: carbon markets and cooperative approaches. Rules were finalised at COP29 (Baku, 2024).
  • Article 7: global goal on adaptation.
  • Article 8: loss and damage.
  • Article 9: finance from developed countries.
  • Article 13: enhanced transparency framework.
  • Article 14: Global Stocktake every five years. The first ended at COP28 (2023).

The Katowice rulebook (COP24, 2018) set the detailed rules. COP26 Glasgow (2021) asked countries to revisit targets and agreed to phase down unabated coal. The Global Stocktake concluded at COP28 (Dubai, 2023) and called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.

By 2025 countries were due to submit new NDCs for 2035. Many were late, and India filed its updated NDC in 2026.

Kyoto was top-down, binding for rich countries only, but limited in reach. Paris is bottom-up and universal, but targets are voluntary and current pledges still point beyond 2 °C without more action.

The US formally left Paris with effect from January 2026 (second time), which weakens finance. Developing countries say CBDR-RC has been diluted.

India ratified Paris in October 2016. It insists on equity, CBDR-RC, a historic responsibility link, climate finance and technology transfer. It supports market mechanisms with safeguards and opposes unilateral carbon border taxes such as the EU’s CBAM.

India’s net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 (2021).

Mains-style: “Compare the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. Which is better for India?” Structure: Kyoto top-down, only Annex I; Paris bottom-up, NDCs; equity and finance; India’s gains (flexibility, space to develop) and risks (pressure to raise targets, CBAM).

Mains-style: “CBDR-RC: is it being diluted?”

Prelims tip: UNFCCC adopted 1992, in force 1994. Kyoto adopted 1997, in force 2005. Paris adopted 2015, in force 2016. CDM is under Kyoto’s Article 12.

Who had binding targets under Kyoto?
quiz.w: Developed countries and economies in transition.

quiz.w: The first was completed at COP28.

quiz.q: The Green Climate Fund was created at:

quiz.w: Article 9 is finance; Article 13 is transparency.
